Hi all, I have the following non-working example followed by a working version:

def B := { x : Nat // x < 2}
-- coercion was always available for subtypes?

instance : CoeOut B Nat := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

instance : CoeOut (List B) (List Nat) := ⟨fun ys => ys.map (fun x => x.val)⟩

def f (x : Nat) (ns : List Nat) (χ : (x y : Nat) → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.map (fun n => χ x n) |>.sum

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys (
    fun x' y' =>
      -- we have to show that x.val = x' here or recover the property from the larger context in some other way
      let x : B := ⟨x', x.property⟩
      let y : B := ⟨y', sorry⟩
      -- asume here we need a function of the richer types or some information on the properties
      if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0
  )
-- a way to make this work so far
def f₀ (x : B) (ys : List B) (χ : (x y : B) → Nat) : Nat :=
   ys.map (fun y => χ x y) |>.sum

def f₀ₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : Nat := f₀ x ys n where
  n (x y : B) : Nat :=
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

In essence I would prefer to not have to specialize f to f₀ just for the sake of the type and I have encountered a frequent usage pattern where we want a theorem or definition to be as general as possible yet, we want to apply it to a richer type. In such cases the information is typically forgotten and I can no longer recover the x.property so reusing this property from the greater context where it is already assumed makes sense while defining f₀ with additional requirements like x.property despite it never being used (and thus part of the expression/statement) seems like a workaround for a limitation.
Can you say what exactly you're trying to achieve and perhaps spend some time producing a #mwe? This would help you pinning down the exact question, and us understanding how we might help.

It is hard to understand what you mean for sure, since when you defined χ as a function of two Nat , so you wouldn't be able to magically recover values of B instead.

For example, x' = 3 and y' = 3 , so it is just in principle not possible to do.

If you start with B you can go Nat like you did in the last line, why is that not what you want?

If you like you can split the cases, and recover a B when you are below 2, but in the other cases you cannot do that because they are simply not a B.

Hmmm, I already provided a #mwe which is exactly what the above is and was translated from a much more complex case to have minimal conceptual overhead. What I am trying to achieve is also already stated in

In essence I would prefer to not have to specialize f to f₀ just for the sake of the type and I have encountered a frequent usage pattern where we want a theorem or definition to be as general as possible yet, we want to apply it to a richer type.

Let me digest and reply in more detail, hopefully I can convey the idea more clearly:

since when you defined χ as a function of two Nat , so you wouldn't be able to magically recover values of B instead.

Exactly, and the reason for this is that χ does not require the additional structure like the additional property and is kept in its most general form down to the minimum number of assumptions/requirements it needs. My desire is not to recover the property and thus the entire B from this function. But I do have more information about my x object outside of the usage of f and would like to use that for proving something about x or in this particular mwe case to apply fₙ (see part "asume here we need a function of the richer types or some information on the properties").

If you start with B you can go Nat like you did in the last line, why is that not what you want?

No and I hope I articulated above why the second example, while solving the issue of definition, is not good enough:

while defining f₀ with additional requirements like x.property despite it never being used (and thus part of the expression/statement) seems like a workaround for a limitation.

Besides being a more boilerplate approach it also requires f₀ to hold assumptions not needed by its implementation like x.property and not be defined in its most general form.

If you like you can split the cases, and recover a B when you are below 2, but in the other cases you cannot do that because they are simply not a B.

One important point of the mwe above is that we are using f strictly in the context of fₙ. So in essence we want f to be as general as possible and require only what it truly needs for its implementation, yet fₙ has additional requirements (added in the B type) and needs to use the general f only some particular purpose then reuse the B terms to complete its own proof or result. We don't want to add irrelevant additions to f just to make it work as in the f₀ case, yet we want fₙ to build on top of the general f and construct the rest of what is needed using the richer (sub)type B.

Plamen Dimitrov said:

But I do have more information about my x object outside of the usage of f and would like to use that for proving something about x

That information can only be obtained from the definition of f, and it is inaccessible from within the function that is passed as an argument to f. Your example can be reduced to:

def f {α β : Type} (x : α) (g : α → β) : β :=
  g x

example : {x // x < 2} :=
  f 1 fun x => ⟨x, sorry⟩ -- There is no way to show `x < 2`

One possible solution is to add a dependent if-then-else and later prove that the condition is always true:

example : {x // x < 2} :=
  f 1 fun x => if h : x < 2 then ⟨x, h⟩ else ⟨0, by decide⟩

In your original example:

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys fun x' y' =>
    if h : x' < 2 ∧ y' < 2 then
      let x : B := ⟨x', h.1⟩
      let y : B := ⟨y', h.2⟩
      if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0
    else 0

fₙ = f₀ₙ

import Mathlib

def B := { x : Nat // x < 2}

instance : CoeOut B Nat := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (List B) (List Nat) := ⟨fun ys => ys.map (fun x => x.val)⟩

def f (x : Nat) (ns : List Nat) (χ : (x y : Nat) → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.map (fun n => χ x n) |>.sum

def f₀ (x : B) (ys : List B) (χ : (x y : B) → Nat) : Nat :=
   ys.map (fun y => χ x y) |>.sum

def f₀ₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : Nat := f₀ x ys n where
  n (x y : B) : Nat :=
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys fun x' y' =>
    if h : x' < 2 ∧ y' < 2 then
      let x : B := ⟨x', h.1⟩
      let y : B := ⟨y', h.2⟩
      if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0
    else 0

@[simp]
theorem flatMap_fn_singleton {α β : Type*} {xs : List α} {f : α → β} :
xs.flatMap ([f ·]) = xs.map f := by
  induction xs; rfl; simp_all

example : fₙ = f₀ₙ := by
  ext; simp [fₙ, f, f₀ₙ, f₀, f₀ₙ.n, Function.comp_def]; grind

Another solution would be to modify f so that it passes additional proofs to χ:

def f (x : Nat) (ns : List Nat) (χ : (x' n : Nat) → x' = x → n ∈ ns → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.attach.map (fun ⟨n, h⟩ => χ x n rfl h) |>.sum

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys fun x' y' h₁ h₂ =>
    let x : B := ⟨x', by grind⟩
    let y : B := ⟨y', by simp at h₂; grind⟩
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

fₙ = f₀ₙ

import Mathlib

def B := { x : Nat // x < 2}

instance : CoeOut B Nat := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (List B) (List Nat) := ⟨fun ys => ys.map (fun x => x.val)⟩

def f (x : Nat) (ns : List Nat) (χ : (x' n : Nat) → x' = x → n ∈ ns → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.attach.map (fun ⟨n, h⟩ => χ x n rfl h) |>.sum

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys fun x' y' h₁ h₂ =>
    let x : B := ⟨x', by grind⟩
    let y : B := ⟨y', by simp at h₂; grind⟩
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

def f₀ (x : B) (ys : List B) (χ : (x y : B) → Nat) : Nat :=
   ys.map (fun y => χ x y) |>.sum

def f₀ₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : Nat := f₀ x ys n where
  n (x y : B) : Nat :=
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

example : fₙ = f₀ₙ := by
  ext x ys; simp [fₙ, f₀ₙ, f₀ₙ.n, f₀, f]
  induction ys; rfl; rename_i y ys ih
  simp; rw! [←ih, List.flatMap_cons]
  simp [Function.comp_def]

This could also be a use case for junk values, so you may also consider the following, which avoids carrying hypothesis directly/immediately but gives a junk value of "(0 : B)" when you don't have a B:

import Mathlib

def B := { x : Nat // x < 2}

instance : CoeOut B Nat := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

instance : CoeOut Nat B := ⟨fun x ↦
  if hb : x < 2 then ⟨x, hb⟩ else ⟨0, by simp⟩⟩

instance : CoeOut (List B) (List Nat) := ⟨fun ys => ys.map (fun x => x.val)⟩

def f (x : Nat) (ns : List Nat) (χ : (x y : Nat) → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.map (fun n => χ x n) |>.sum

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys (
    fun x' y' =>
      let x : B := ↑x'
      let y : B := ↑y'
      if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0
  )

Probably may not want both of those to be going through instances of coercions though.

I am also surprised a little bit that given an instance of CoeOut foo bar we don't get a canonical instance of CoeOut (List foo) (List bar).

Thanks both for the follow-ups.

One possible solution is to add a dependent if-then-else and later prove that the condition is always true:

This is a way to generate that information and in some cases irrelevant values like zero and doesn't satisfy the requirement from the original goal of reusing the information already provided via the B types. In other words, the are already given that x' < 2 as x.property and similarly but a bit more long-winded-ly for n.

Edit: I just realised this is essentially the same as above :man_facepalming:

Indeed, I guess the right way to call such values is junk values then.

Another solution would be to modify f so that it passes additional proofs to χ:

This is indeed getting much closer to the crux of the goal here. It does exactly use the information we are already given and doesn't generate any new information just to satisfy the requirement to know the property. This was my original point that the larger context of fₙ already requires and thus provides the · < 2 property and we simply want to relate x and x' and similarly for the list case.

The price to pay here is in losing generality of the domain of application of χ which now requires more structure to apply even though f is kept as general as before (requiring only Nat and not its subtype B with the richer structure). It therefore only moves the problem around by now requiring additional properties to pass to χ which definitely fit well with the example for χ above like

def χ := fun x' y' h₁ h₂ =>
    let x : B := ⟨x', by grind⟩
    let y : B := ⟨y', by simp at h₂; grind⟩
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

but will not allow using f with a different χ if we don't need the · < 2 property in another case and still want to reuse a general f. So if ⟨a, b⟩ is more general and requires less structure than ⟨a, b, c⟩ and a than ⟨a, b⟩ then I guess the only way to increase the generality ever further would be to escalate to higher universe so that we don't even ask the question whether there is additional b property or not:

import Mathlib

def B := { x : Nat // x < 2}

instance : CoeOut B Nat := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (List B) (List Nat) := ⟨fun ys => ys.map (fun x => x.val)⟩

def f (x : α) (ns : List α) (χ : α → α → Nat) : Nat :=
  ns.map (fun n => χ x n) |>.sum

def fₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : ℕ :=
  f x ys fun x' y' =>
    let x : B := x'
    let y : B := y'
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

def f₀ (x : B) (ys : List B) (χ : (x y : B) → Nat) : Nat :=
   ys.map (fun y => χ x y) |>.sum

def f₀ₙ (x : B) (ys : List B) : Nat := f₀ x ys n where
  n (x y : B) : Nat :=
    if x.val + y.val = 3 then 1 else 0

I guess this was a much simpler question than I originally thought in which case I would say that @Vlad's answer is still most accurate for localizing the required structure better while still providing a solution for the original construction.
